ownership_analysis.text:
# Independent ownership review

The ownership state is local to one invocation, rather than a global circuit flag. The existing service RLock serializes caller cancellation and target entry. Only pending belongs to the caller; target entry changes it to running, and caller failure does not release running or finished. A canceled late target exits before helper import or runtime access. The worker's cleanup covers its setup and owns the single running-to-finished release. Join timeout does not reclaim the worker's lease.

Registration and start remain in one critical section, so close's same-lock snapshot cannot see an unstarted registration. In the reviewed [CPython3.12 threading implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/python/cpython/3.12/Lib/threading.py), start waits for a bootstrap event, which is set before the target is invoked. Thus the worker's acquisition of the service lock does not itself create a start-waits-for-target lock cycle in that implementation. This is source evidence, not a real-thread experiment or a claim covering every Python implementation.

The corrected fake covers completion before a start exception, late canceled delivery, delayed live timeout, setup failure and deterministic close ordering. The running-but-incomplete argument is the local-state/lock invariant above; the sequential fake does not execute real overlap. Arbitrary signal interruption inside lock/release primitives, MemoryError at every allocation and shutdown timing remain outside the proof.

The v1 close oracle could reject a valid synchronous completion because it demanded observing an already-finished registration. Before production patching, it was replaced with a started target delivered on first join. The old runner and setup/error logs were preserved; the corrected v2 bytes stayed unchanged before and after the production patch.
